entities.name: The Art of War (Sunzi Bingfa)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Attributed to the Chinese general Sun Tzu (Sun Wu), written during the late Spring and Autumn period or early Warring States period (c. 5th century BCE), The Art of War is the most influential military treatise in East Asian history and arguably the most widely read strategy text in the world. In 13 laconic chapters (approximately 6,000 Chinese characters), Sun Tzu sets forth principles of warfare that transcend their military origins to become universal maxims of strategy: "All warfare is based on deception"; "The supreme art of war is to subdue the enemy without fighting"; "Know your enemy and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you will not be in peril." Unlike Western military writers who focus on battle tactics, Sun Tzu emphasizes intelligence, deception, psychological manipulation, and strategic positioning — making conflict resolution through combat a last resort.

The work profoundly influenced Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese military doctrine for 2,500 years, and since its introduction to Europe (1772) has been adopted by business strategists, diplomats, and sports coaches worldwide. The 1972 discovery of the Yinqueshan Han bamboo slips confirmed the text's antiquity.
